etymology: From the Old English hap (chance, fortune, that which befalls), by way of the Norse happ; with the adverbial ending it means ‘by hap,’ perchance, if it so fall out.
biblical_def: To do a thing haply is to do it in hope of a chance not yet secured — ‘if perchance,’ ‘it may be.’ The word marks the difference between the LORD’s certainty and man’s uncertainty. When our Lord came to the fig tree, He came “if haply he might find any thing thereon” (Mar 11:13), and found only leaves — a parable of fruitless profession judged. Gamaliel warns the council that in fighting the apostles they may “haply” be found fighting against God (Act 5:39), a hesitance that yet trembles before providence. Paul at Athens declares that God set the bounds of the nations “that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him” (Act 17:27) — the groping of the blind after a God near at hand. Jonathan laments how much greater the slaughter had been “if haply the people had eaten” (1Sa 14:30). In every place the word confesses the creature’s ignorance of the issue. Yet the seeking is not vain: what man attempts perchance, God has ordained certainly. The elect feel after Him haply and find Him surely, for He is not far, and the seeking itself is His gift. The word humbles the searcher and magnifies the sovereign Lord who is found.
webster_summary: By hap or chance; perhaps; peradventure; it may be.
webster_full: HAPLY, adv. [from hap, chance.] By chance; perhaps; it may be; peradventure.
Used to introduce a thing whose issue is uncertain to the doer: as, he sought, if haply he might find.
It expresses a contingency depending not on the will of the speaker but on the event, and so confesses his ignorance of what shall be.
In Scripture it often marks the seeking of God by men who know not whether they shall find, though He is near.
Distinguished from a bare wish: it looks toward an outcome possible but not promised to the seeker.
scriptures: And seeing a fig tree afar off having leaves, he came, if haply he might find any thing thereon
Act 5:39
But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:
How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? for had there not been now a much greater slaughter among the Philistines?
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a lost adverb; ‘haply’ recovers the honest uncertainty of the creature who seeks a God he cannot command.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the word rebukes is presumption — the modern habit of treating tomorrow as owned and God as at our disposal. “Haply” puts the creature back in his place: he may seek, he may feel after, but the finding is not in his hand. James rebukes the same presumption when men say they will buy and sell and get gain, who know not what shall be on the morrow (Jas 4:14). The word teaches a reverent tentativeness before providence — not despair, but the humility that says ‘if the Lord will.’

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is subtler: modern versions render the word away, and with it goes the KJV’s fine confession that the seeker gropes and the finder is found by grace. Recover the principle that man seeks haply and God is found certainly — the very structure of Act 17:27, where blind feeling after God meets a God who is not far. Our uncertainty and His nearness are not enemies; the one drives us to the other.
roots_summary: One English root — hap, that which befalls — underlies a family of words the KJV still keeps.
roots_lines: hap (Old English, from Norse happ) — chance, fortune, that which falls out; the bare event apart from man’s design.
haply — by hap; perchance; the adverb of contingency the KJV sets before uncertain seeking.
happen, hapless, mishap, perhaps — the same root, still living, though ‘haply’ alone keeps the old reverent flavor.
The Greek behind Act 17:27 is ei ara ge — ‘if indeed then,’ the very grammar of tentative seeking.
The word never means blind luck in Scripture: what befalls man haply befalls him under a providence that ordained it (Pro 16:33).
usage: He came seeking fruit haply, and found only leaves: profession without fruit is judged.
We feel after God haply; He was never far, and the finding is His gift.
Say not ‘I will,’ but ‘if the Lord will’ — the haply of a humble heart.

etymology: From the Middle English privé (private, secret), through Old French from the Latin privatus (withdrawn from public life); the adverb means secretly, in a hidden or stealthy manner.
biblical_def: Privily means secretly, covertly, by stealth — the opposite of openly. Scripture uses it two ways, and the difference is the whole moral weight of the word. The wicked act privily for evil: they “privily shoot at the upright in heart” (Psa 11:2), bending the bow in the dark; false brethren “came in privily to spy out our liberty” (Gal 2:4), infiltrators against the gospel of grace. Secrecy here is the native air of malice, which cannot bear the light (Joh 3:20). But the word also serves mercy: Joseph, a just man unwilling to shame Mary, “was minded to put her away privily” (Mat 1:19) — privacy as tenderness, covering rather than exposing. And Paul at Philippi refuses to be thrust out privily (Act 16:37), demanding the magistrates own their wrong openly, for the gospel’s honor. So the same secrecy is now the cloak of the assassin, now the courtesy of the merciful, now the injustice a servant of Christ may lawfully resist. The lesson is that the hidden thing takes its character from the heart. God sees in secret (Mat 6:4); nothing is privily done before Him. What men do in the dark against the upright, He beholds; what the merciful do quietly for the guilty, He rewards openly.
webster_summary: Secretly; privately; in a hidden or stealthy manner, not openly.
webster_full: PRIVILY, adv. [from privy, Latin privatus.] Secretly; privately; not openly; by stealth.
To do a thing privily is to do it out of sight, whether from shame, from malice, or from a merciful desire not to expose.
In an ill sense, the manner of the plotter, the slanderer, and the false teacher who creeps in unawares.
In a good sense, the manner of the tender, who would spare the guilty an open shame.
Opposed to openly: the word turns the mind at once to the question, why is this hidden?
scriptures: Psa 11:2
For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart.
Mat 1:19
Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.
And now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out.
Gal 2:4
And that because of false brethren unawares brought in, who came in privily to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage:
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under attack but a searching word; ‘privily’ presses the question the age evades — what is done in secret, and why?
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the love of the hidden sin — the compromise kept privily, the bow bent in the dark against a brother’s name. Our age has perfected private wickedness: the concealed habit, the anonymous slander, the false teacher who creeps in privily under fair words. Scripture answers that secrecy alters nothing before the God who is light: “there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed” (Mat 10:26). Yet the same word blesses a holy secrecy — the alms done privily, the fault covered in love — and so it divides the darkness that hides shame from the darkness that spares it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What is lost is the KJV’s precise moral probe: modern renderings say ‘secretly’ and lose nothing of sense but something of edge. Recover the principle that the hidden thing is never hidden from God, and that the character of a secret act is fixed by the heart behind it — malice or mercy, the assassin’s privacy or Joseph’s.
roots_summary: The root is privé, that which is withdrawn from the public — whence privy, private, privilege, and privily.
roots_lines: privatus (Latin) — withdrawn from public office or view; the private as opposed to the public thing.
privé (Old French / Middle English) — secret, intimate, familiar; the immediate parent of the English word.
privy — privy to a matter, made a secret sharer; whence privily, in the manner of the privy.
Kin: private, privilege, privity, deprive — all turning on the drawing of a thing apart from the common eye.
Scripture’s two uses — Psa 11:2 (malice) and Mat 1:19 (mercy) — show the neutral root taking its color from the heart.
usage: The slanderer shoots privily; God sees the bow bent in the dark.
Joseph would put her away privily — secrecy can be the dress of mercy.
Ask of every hidden act the plain question: why is this done privily?

etymology: From the Old English thriga / thriwa (three times), which took the Middle English adverbial genitive -s to become thries, then thrice: literally ‘three times.’
biblical_def: Thrice is simply ‘three times,’ but in Scripture the number rarely counts idly; it presses toward completeness, solemn confirmation, or hard trial. Our Lord foretold, “before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mat 26:34), and the threefold denial — matched afterward by a threefold “lovest thou me” — makes Peter’s fall complete and his restoration equally full (Joh 13:38; Joh 21:17). Three times a year all Israel’s males were to appear before the LORD (Exo 34:23), the appointed feasts binding the year to worship. Paul, numbering his sufferings, was “thrice” beaten with rods and “thrice” he suffered shipwreck (2Co 11:25), and thrice besought the Lord about his thorn (2Co 12:8). The word gathers the weight of a thing done to the full: a denial thrice is no slip but a settled failure; a beating thrice is no accident but a pattern of affliction; an appearing thrice a year is a rhythm of covenant devotion. Yet mark the mercy — where sin abounded thrice, grace abounded to restore thrice; where the servant suffered thrice, the Lord’s grace was sufficient. The number that measures Peter’s shame measures also his recommissioning. Thrice teaches that God counts our falls exactly, and answers them with a completeness of grace that overtops the completeness of our sin.
webster_summary: Three times; and figuratively, to the full, or with emphasis.
webster_full: THRICE, adv. [Old English thriga, three times.] Three times.
Used to number a thing done three several times: as, he denied thrice.
By a common idiom, put for completeness or emphasis, as we say thrice-blessed, thrice-happy.
In Scripture it marks solemn repetition — the three yearly feasts, the threefold denial, the thrice-besought petition.
Distinct from a vague ‘often’: it counts exactly, and the exact count carries the meaning.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
Thrice in the year shall all your men children appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel.
Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;
Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.
corruption_summary: Not a disputed word but a counted one; ‘thrice’ recovers the exactness with which Scripture numbers both our falls and God’s mercies.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes our vagueness about sin. We prefer to say we failed ‘a few times,’ blurring the count; Scripture says Peter denied his Lord thrice, and will not let the number soften. God keeps precise books. Yet the same exactness is our comfort: He who counted the three denials counted also the three restorations, and the servant beaten thrice was upheld by a grace measured to the need. To lose the word is to lose the discipline of naming sin by its true number and mercy by its true measure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern speech simply drops the word for ‘three times,’ a small loss of cadence — but with it can go the biblical habit of exact reckoning. Recover the principle that God numbers precisely: our falls are neither exaggerated nor excused, and His grace answers each by count, restoring Peter as many times as he denied.
roots_summary: An Old English numeral adverb, thriga, that took the -s of the adverbial genitive and came down to us as thrice.
roots_lines: thriga / thriwa (Old English) — three times; the base numeral three made adverbial.
-s (adverbial genitive) — the same ending that gives once and twice, whence thries, then thrice.
Kin: once, twice, thrice — the old counted adverbs, of which thrice is the last still bearing an archaic ring.
Behind Mat 26:34 the Greek is simply tris — three times — plain in count, heavy in sense.
Scripture’s threes are seldom idle: feast, denial, and petition all use the number for solemn fulness.
usage: He denied thrice and was restored thrice: God answers our falls by count.
Thrice a year Israel appeared before the LORD — devotion has a rhythm.
Paul besought the Lord thrice, and learned that grace, not removal, was the answer.

etymology: From the Middle English bitimes — bi (by) plus time with the adverbial -s — meaning ‘by the time,’ that is, early, in good season, betimes.
biblical_def: Betimes means early, seasonably, in good time — and by extension diligently, without delay. The picture behind it is the man who rises with the dawn to be about his business. Isaac and Abimelech “rose up betimes in the morning” to swear their covenant (Gen 26:31); the diligent begin their weightiest work early. The word rises to its height in the LORD’s own dealing: He “sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending” (2Ch 36:15), an image of God as one who rises early, again and again, pleading with a rebellious people through His prophets — long-suffering pictured as unwearied earliness. Bildad counsels Job, “If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes” (Job 8:5), for the seeking of God is not to be deferred to the evening of life. And Solomon: “he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes” (Pro 13:24) — love disciplines a child early, while the twig is bent, not late when the tree is set. So the word gathers a whole doctrine of timeliness: God seeks us betimes, therefore we must seek Him betimes; the father corrects betimes because delayed discipline is cruelty dressed as kindness. To do a thing betimes is to honor the hour God gives, before the day is spent and the season past. “To day if ye will hear his voice” (Heb 3:15) is the gospel of betimes.
webster_summary: Seasonably; early; in good time; soon; before it is late.
webster_full: BETIMES, adv. [be, by, and time.] Seasonably; in good season or time; before it is late.
Early in the day: as, he rose betimes in the morning.
Soon; in a short time; without delay: as, seek the Lord betimes.
By an easy extension, diligently and repeatedly, as of one who begins early and holds to it.
Opposed to lateness and delay: it commends the honoring of the hour before it is spent.
scriptures: And they rose up betimes in the morning, and sware one to another: and Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.
And the LORD God of their fathers sent to them by his messengers, rising up betimes, and sending; because he had compassion on his people, and on his dwelling place:
Job 8:5
If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty;
He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.
corruption_summary: Not a redefined term but a forgotten discipline; ‘betimes’ recovers the urgency of the early hour — God’s in pleading, ours in seeking and correcting.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes delay. Our age counsels waiting — put off repentance, put off correction, keep the child’s will unbroken and call it kindness. Scripture rises early: God sent His prophets rising up betimes, and the father who loves chastens betimes, while there is yet time to bend the will toward good. To defer the seeking of God to the last hour presumes upon a morrow not promised; to defer the correction of a child until habit hardens is not gentleness but neglect. The gospel word is to day, not tomorrow.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is the loss of urgency: modern speech says ‘early’ and keeps the sense but drops the moral summons the KJV carries in ‘betimes.’ Recover the principle that grace has a season and duty an hour: God pleads betimes and calls us to seek, obey, and correct betimes, before the day is far spent.
roots_summary: A plain compound — by-time-s — that the KJV keeps as a summons to the early and seasonable hour.
roots_lines: be- (Old English bi) — by, at, near; the same prefix as in before, beside, between.
time — the appointed hour or season; the heart of the word.
-s — the adverbial ending, as in always, needs, unawares; making ‘by-time’ into an adverb of manner.
So betimes = ‘by the time,’ in season, early — and thence, of one who begins early, diligently.
The Hebrew behind 2Ch 36:15 is shakam, to rise early — the very picture of God rising betimes to plead.
usage: Seek God betimes; the last hour is a poor place to begin.
He that loveth his child chasteneth him betimes — delayed discipline is cruelty.
God rose up betimes to send His prophets; slight not His early mercy.

etymology: From the Old English syndrig (separate, distinct, several), from sundor (apart, asunder); hence ‘sundry’ = various, several, of separate kinds.
biblical_def: Sundry means several, various, of separate and distinct kinds — things taken apart one from another rather than lumped together. Its great use stands at the head of Hebrews: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets” (Heb 1:1). ‘At sundry times’ renders a single Greek word meaning ‘in many parts, piecemeal’ — the old revelation came not all at once but portion by portion, to Abraham a promise, to Moses a law, to David a psalm, to Isaiah a vision, each a separate parcel of light (Num 12:6). The word thus confesses the fragmentary, progressive character of the former age: true, holy, God-breathed, yet given in pieces and by many hands. But the sentence does not rest there. “Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son” (Heb 1:2): the sundry portions find their sum in One. Where prophecy was many and partial, the Son is single and full — not another parcel but the whole, not a further fragment but the Word made flesh in whom all the fragments cohere (Luk 24:27). So ‘sundry’ is a gospel word by contrast: it measures the manifold preparation against the single perfection of Christ. The many times were real; the last days are final. God spoke in sundry parts that we might prize the one entire Speech, His Son.
webster_summary: Several; various; more than one or two; of separate and distinct kinds.
webster_full: SUNDRY, a. [Old English syndrig, from sundor, apart.] Several; divers; more than one; of distinct kinds.
Taken severally, one apart from another, not in a mass: as, sundry persons, sundry times.
It regards things as separate and distinguished, whereas ‘many’ regards them only as numerous.
In Heb 1:1, ‘at sundry times’ renders the sense of piecemeal, part after part, the old revelation given in portions.
Kin in meaning to divers, with which the KJV pairs it: at sundry times and in divers manners.
scriptures: Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
Heb 1:2
Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son, whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds;
Num 12:6
And he said, Hear now my words: If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision, and will speak unto him in a dream.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a fading word; ‘sundry’ recovers the piecemeal way God spake of old and the single perfection of His last Word, the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the appetite for the many at the cost of the One. Our age loves the sundry — a thousand voices, endless partial insights, revelation scattered and never summed — and grows deaf to the single Speech that gathers all. Scripture honors the sundry times, the true and holy fragments given to the fathers; but it bends them all toward Christ, in whom the parcels of promise cohere. To rest in sundry fragments and refuse the whole Word made flesh is to stop at the shadow when the substance has come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has merely grown quaint, kept alive in ‘sundry’ and ‘all and sundry.’ Recover the doctrine it carries: God spake progressively and in parts, and then finally and fully in His Son. The sundry times were preparation; the last days are fulfilment, and the many fragments have one entire meaning, which is Christ.
roots_summary: From sundor, apart — the same root that gives asunder, sunder, and sundry, all of things set severally apart.
roots_lines: sundor (Old English) — apart, separately; the base sense of severalness.
syndrig — separate, distinct, several; the immediate parent of ‘sundry.’
Kin: sunder, asunder, sundry — all of the setting of things apart one from another.
The Greek of Heb 1:1 is polumeros, ‘in many parts’ — revelation given piece by piece.
Paired with polutropos, ‘in many manners’ (divers), it frames the whole preparation before the Son.
usage: God spake in sundry parts of old; He has spoken in one Son at last.
Prize the many prophets, but rest in the single Word made flesh.
The sundry fragments of promise cohere in Christ alone.

etymology: From the Old French divers, Latin diversus (turned different ways, apart), the past participle of divertere; ‘divers’ means various, sundry, of differing kinds.
biblical_def: Divers means various, several, of differing kinds — not the modern ‘diverse’ with its freight of ideology, but the plain old word for many and unlike. It heads Hebrews beside its fellow: God spake “in divers manners” of old (Heb 1:1), in vision, dream, law, and prophecy, many modes for one message, until the Son spake all in Himself. It names the press of human misery brought to Christ: they brought Him “all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments” (Mat 4:24), and He healed them — every kind of affliction meeting one Physician. It marks the far-come crowd: “divers of them came from far” (Mar 8:3), and He would not send them fasting away. And James turns the word to the school of faith: “count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations” (Jas 1:2) — trials of many kinds, come not by chance but for the proving of faith and the working of patience. So ‘divers’ teaches the manifoldness of things beneath one governing hand: many manners of revelation, one Word; many diseases, one Healer; many temptations, one purpose — that the tried faith, more precious than gold, be found unto praise. The variety is real; the sovereignty over it is total. God’s people meet divers trials, but not a divers God: He is one, and works all the manifold to a single, gracious end.
webster_summary: Various; several; sundry; of differing kinds or sorts.
webster_full: DIVERS, a. [Latin diversus.] Several; sundry; more than one; various.
Different in kind; of many sorts: as, divers diseases, divers manners.
An old collective, regarding things as many and unlike, without the modern ideological sense of ‘diverse.’
Paired in Heb 1:1 with sundry: God spake at sundry times and in divers manners.
Distinguished from ‘diverse’ in spelling and use, though of one root: ‘divers’ means simply various.
scriptures: Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
Mat 4:24

And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them.
Jas 1:2
My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations;
Mar 8:3
And if I send them away fasting to their own houses, they will faint by the way: for divers of them came from far.
corruption_summary: Not a redefined doctrine but a word shadowed by its modern cousin; ‘divers’ recovers the plain sense of many and unlike — and the one hand over the manifold.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes no single heresy, but its modern echo ‘diversity’ has crowded out the older, humbler sense. ‘Divers’ simply means various — divers diseases, divers manners, divers temptations — and it always looks past the variety to the God who governs it. The temptation of the age is to prize variety as an end, to worship the manifold for its own sake; Scripture prizes the One over the many, the single Word behind the divers manners, the one Physician for the divers diseases. Count it all joy in divers temptations not because trials are good in themselves, but because one wise hand works them all for the proving of faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word itself is not contested; it has merely faded, and readers now hear its cousin ‘diverse’ where the KJV said ‘divers.’ Recover the plain meaning — various, of many kinds — and the doctrine it serves: beneath every divers manner and divers trial stands one God, working the manifold to a single end (Rom 8:28).
roots_summary: From the Latin diversus, turned different ways — the old ‘divers’ and the modern ‘diverse’ are one root, two paths.
roots_lines: divertere (Latin) — to turn apart, turn different ways; whence diversus, turned aside, differing.
divers (Old French / Middle English) — various, several, sundry; the KJV’s plain collective.
diverse — the same word respelled, now bearing a weight of modern meaning the KJV never intended.
Kin: divert, diverse, diversity, divorce — all of the turning-apart of the root.
In Heb 1:1 the Greek is polutropos, ‘in many manners’ — the manifold modes of one revelation.
usage: God spake in divers manners; the manifold ways served one message.
Divers diseases met one Physician, and He healed them all.
Count it joy in divers temptations: one hand works them to a single end.

etymology: From the verb noise (Middle English, from Old French noise, an outcry or brawl); ‘to be noised’ is to be spread abroad by report, rumored, made loud in the common talk.
biblical_def: To be noised is to be spread abroad by report, to become the loud talk of a place. It is the passive of rumor — a thing so striking it will not stay quiet. After Jericho fell, “the fame of Joshua was noised throughout all the country” (Jos 6:27), the LORD’s victory carrying His servant’s name on every tongue. When Christ returned to Capernaum, “it was noised that he was in the house” (Mar 2:1), and the press of hearers was such that four men tore up a roof. At John’s birth the wondrous sayings “were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea” (Luk 1:65), for God’s visitations cannot be hid. And at Pentecost, “when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together” (Act 2:6), the sound of the Spirit gathering the nations to hear. Mark the pattern: in every place it is the works of God that get noised — a city taken, a Healer come, a forerunner born, a Church baptized in fire. The gospel is not a private thing; where God acts, report runs. Yet the word warns as well as invites: rumor magnifies without discerning, and the crowd that is noised together may come to gape as easily as to believe. The believer’s calling is not merely to help noise the report but to hear it unto faith — for the same tidings that gather a curious multitude are the power of God unto them that are called.
webster_summary: Spread abroad by report; rumored; made the subject of common talk.
webster_full: NOISE, v.t. To spread by rumor or report. Usually in the passive, to be noised.
To be talked of loudly and widely, as tidings that will not be kept quiet.
Formed from the noun noise, an outcry, din, or loud report of a multitude.
In Scripture always of a thing striking enough to run of itself: a victory, a healing, a birth, a wonder.
Distinguished from mere ‘telling’: it implies the swift, unbidden spread of report through a whole country.
scriptures: Jos 6:27
So the LORD was with Joshua; and his fame was noised throughout all the country.
Mar 2:1
And again he entered into Capernaum after some days; and it was noised that he was in the house.
Luk 1:65
And fear came on all that dwelt round about them: and all these sayings were noised abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea.
Act 2:6
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a lost verb; ‘noised’ recovers the truth that the works of God will not be hushed — and that a noised report is not yet a believing heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a double fault: the love of noise for its own sake, and the mistaking of report for faith. Our age is noised with everything and settled in nothing; rumor runs and hearts remain unmoved. Scripture’s ‘noised’ is different — it is the works of God breaking out because they cannot be contained, a city taken, a Saviour come. Yet even there the multitude noised together at Pentecost was ‘confounded,’ not yet converted; the report must be heard unto faith. To hear the gospel noised and go home unchanged is the peril the word exposes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern speech keeps ‘noise’ only as din and loses the fine old sense of a report spread abroad. Recover the principle that God’s mighty acts get themselves noised of their own weight — and that the calling of the hearer is not to swell the rumor but to believe the thing reported.
roots_summary: The noun noise — an outcry of a crowd — turned verb, to spread a thing loudly abroad.
roots_lines: noise (Old French) — a brawl, outcry, or loud din of many voices; the raw material of rumor.
As a verb, to noise — to make loud, to publish by report; chiefly passive, to be noised.
Beware the false friend: noisome (noxious) is of a different root and unrelated in sense.
The Greek behind Mar 2:1 and Act 2:6 is simply ‘it was heard’ — the report went out and was heard of all.
Scripture’s usage is uniform: what is noised is a work of God too great to keep silence.
usage: The victory was the LORD’s, yet Joshua’s fame was noised abroad.
It was noised that Christ was in the house — and the roof came off for it.
A gospel noised in your ears is not yet a gospel believed in your heart.

etymology: From the French bruit, a noise or report, from Old French bruire (to roar, to make a din); a bruit is a rumor, a report, the noised tidings of a thing.
biblical_def: A bruit is a report, a rumor, the noised tidings of some great and commonly dreadful thing. The word appears but twice in the KJV, and both times it carries the sound of coming judgment. Jeremiah cries, “Behold, the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah desolate” (Jer 10:22) — the rumor of the invader running before his armies, the very report a terror. And Nahum, pronouncing Nineveh’s doom, says, “all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee” (Nah 3:19) — the report of the tyrant’s fall greeted with applause by the nations he had ground down. So the bruit is tidings that travel ahead of a fate: in Judah, the dread of judgment approaching; in Nineveh, the joy of judgment fallen. Scripture treats such reports soberly. “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exo 23:1); and the righteous man “shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD” (Psa 112:7). Here is the believer’s stay against every fearful bruit: rumors of war and ruin may run, and the wicked have cause to dread the report of their end, but the man whose heart is fixed on God need not be moved by the loudest rumor. The bruit that terrifies the guilty cannot unsettle the trusting.
webster_summary: Report; rumor; noised tidings, commonly of some fearful or notable event.
webster_full: BRUIT, n. [French bruit, a noise.] Report; rumor; fame; the noised tidings of a thing.
The loud running of a report through a country, especially of war, disaster, or a great man’s fall.
BRUIT, v.t. To report; to noise abroad; to spread the rumor of.
Akin in sense to fame and rumor, but with the ring of a din or outcry in it.
In Scripture, twice used, and both of a dreadful report — Judah’s invader and Nineveh’s downfall.
scriptures: Behold, the noise of the bruit is come, and a great commotion out of the north country, to make the cities of Judah desolate, and a den of dragons.
Nah 3:19
There is no healing of thy bruise; thy wound is grievous: all that hear the bruit of thee shall clap the hands over thee: for upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?
Exo 23:1
Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD.
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine in dispute but a vanished word; ‘bruit’ recovers the fixed heart that fears no evil tidings because it trusts the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the fear that feeds on rumor. Our age is drowned in bruits — every hour a fresh report of alarm, and hearts made captive to tidings they cannot verify or govern. Scripture does not deny that dreadful reports come; Judah heard the bruit of the north and it was real. But it forbids the false report (Exo 23:1) and fortifies the believer against the true one: ‘his heart is fixed, trusting in the LORD’ (Psa 112:7). The wicked have cause to dread the bruit of their end; the child of God, though he hear the loudest rumor, is not moved, for his life is hid in One the rumor cannot reach.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply fallen out of use, and with it a vivid name for the running of fearful report. Recover the principle beneath it: evil tidings will come, but a heart fixed on the LORD is not to be shaken by any bruit, and false reports are not to be raised or received.
roots_summary: A French word for noise and report, come whole into English and kept only in the KJV and the old speech.
roots_lines: bruire (Old French) — to roar, rustle, make a din; the sound behind the word.
bruit (French noun) — noise, and thence rumor or report; borrowed unchanged into English.
Kin in idea: rumor, fame, report, tidings — all of a thing spread by hearsay.
The Hebrew behind Jer 10:22 (shemuah) and Nah 3:19 (shema) means simply ‘a thing heard,’ a report.
Both biblical uses are of judgment — dreaded as it approaches, applauded when it falls on the tyrant.
usage: The bruit of the invader ran before his armies, and Judah trembled.
All that heard the bruit of Nineveh’s fall clapped their hands.
Let the bruits run: the heart fixed on the LORD is not afraid of evil tidings.

etymology: From the Old English metan (to measure, to mark out), kin to the German messen; to mete is to measure, to deal out by measure, to apportion.
biblical_def: To mete is to measure, to deal out by measure, to apportion with a rule. The word carries a double freight in Scripture: it names both God’s incomprehensible measuring of creation and the measure a man deals to his neighbor. Our Lord lays down the law of just recompense: “with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again” (Mat 7:2), and again, “with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given” (Mar 4:24). The rule a man uses on others God will use on him — harsh judgment earns harsh judgment, generous measure earns overflowing return. This is not mechanical fate but the moral order of a righteous God. Then the word soars: the LORD “meted out heaven with the span” (Isa 40:12), measuring the very heavens with the breadth of His hand, weighing the mountains in scales — an image to shrink every proud measurer to dust. And He who metes the heavens says, “I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth” (Psa 60:6), portioning the land to His people by sovereign right. So ‘mete’ joins two truths: the God who measures out the cosmos will not be mismeasured by man, and He holds us to the measure we deal others. Measure mercy, and mercy is meted back; measure the span of heaven, and be still before the hand that fills it.
webster_summary: To measure; to deal or distribute by measure; to apportion.
webster_full: METE, v.t. [Old English metan, to measure.] To measure; to ascertain quantity or extent by a rule or standard.
To deal out or distribute by measure; to apportion: as, to mete out a portion.
Used of God’s measuring of creation: to mete out heaven with the span.
Used of man’s dealing with man: the measure he metes shall be meted to him.
METE, n. A measure, bound, or limit; whence ‘metes and bounds.’
scriptures: Mat 7:2
For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
Mar 4:24
And he said unto them, Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given.
Psa 60:6
God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth.

Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
corruption_summary: Not a redefined term but a lost measuring-word; ‘mete’ recovers the twofold truth — God measures all things, and metes to us the measure we deal others.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the man who metes one measure to others and demands another for himself. Our age is loud in judgment and thin in mercy, quick to mete out condemnation while pleading exception for its own. Christ closes that door: ‘with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again’ (Mat 7:2). The rule you press upon your brother is the rule God will press upon you. And behind the warning stands the greatness of the Measurer, who meted out heaven with a span (Isa 40:12) — how shall the creature who cannot measure a handful of dust set himself up to mete harsh judgment on his fellow?

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern usage keeps ‘mete out’ only in the phrase ‘mete out punishment,’ losing the older breadth of simple measuring. Recover the principle the word holds together: the God who metes the heavens holds us to the measure we mete to men — therefore deal mercy, that mercy be meted back.
roots_summary: One old English verb of measuring, metan, still living in ‘mete out’ and in ‘metes and bounds.’
roots_lines: metan (Old English) — to measure, to mark out; kin to German messen, to measure.
mete (verb) — to measure, to deal out by measure; the KJV’s word for both divine and human measuring.
mete (noun) — a bound or limit set by measuring; surviving in ‘metes and bounds.’
The Hebrew of Isa 40:12 (takan) means to weigh or adjust by measure — the LORD gauging the heavens.
The Greek of Mat 7:2 (metreo) is the plain verb to measure, whence our ‘metre’ and ‘measure.’
usage: The measure you mete to others is the measure God will mete to you.
He meted out heaven with a span — be still, and let Him measure.
Mete mercy, and look for mercy meted back, pressed down and running over.

etymology: From the Old French menuisier and Latin minuere (to make small, lessen); ‘minish’ is the older, shorter form of ‘diminish,’ to make less, to reduce.
biblical_def: To minish is to make less, to lessen, to reduce — the elder and shorter brother of ‘diminish.’ It appears twice in the KJV, and both times it names a cruel reduction of what men need to live. Under Pharaoh’s lash the officers heard, “Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task” (Exo 5:19): the quota was not to be lessened though the straw was taken away — oppression that increases the burden while cutting the means. And the psalmist, tracing the LORD’s dealings with the proud, sings that “they are minished and brought low through oppression, affliction, and sorrow” (Psa 107:39): here God Himself minishes, bringing the mighty down, that He may lift the needy from affliction. So the word cuts two ways. In Pharaoh’s mouth, to minish is tyranny — the strong wringing more from the weak. In God’s hand, to minish is judgment and mercy joined — He minishes the oppressor to relieve the oppressed. Scripture guards the word’s solemnity in a third place: “neither shall ye diminish ought” from His commandment (Deu 4:2), and he that takes away from the words of the prophecy shall have his part taken away (Rev 22:19). What God has given, man may not minish; what man has usurped, God will. To minish God’s word is deadly; to be minished by His hand, if it lay us low that He may raise us, is grace in a severe dress.
webster_summary: To make less; to lessen; to diminish; the older form of diminish.
webster_full: MINISH, v.t. [Latin minuere, to lessen.] To make less; to lessen; to diminish.
The older and shorter form, of which ‘diminish’ (with the prefix di-) is the enlarged descendant.
To reduce in number, quantity, or measure: as, to minish the tale of bricks.
Used both of unjust reduction, as by an oppressor, and of the LORD’s bringing low of the proud.
Kin: minute, minor, minish, diminish — all of the Latin root for smallness.
scriptures: Exo 5:19
And the officers of the children of Israel did see that they were in evil case, after it was said, Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task.
Again, they are minished and brought low through oppression, affliction, and sorrow.
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.

And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book.
corruption_summary: Not a doctrine under attack but a discarded word; ‘minish’ recovers the sober truth that God brings the proud low and forbids the paring-down of His word.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes two abiding sins: the oppressor who minishes the portion of the weak, and the reviser who minishes the word of God. Pharaoh minished neither quota while taking the straw — the pattern of every tyranny that demands more and gives less. And the age is full of hands that would minish Scripture, taking away the hard sayings, the wrath, the exclusive Christ, until a smaller gospel remains. Against both stands the warning: ‘neither shall ye diminish ought’ (Deu 4:2), and God shall take away the part of him that takes away from His words (Rev 22:19). What He has spoken, none may lessen and live.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply yielded to its longer form ‘diminish,’ a small loss of the KJV’s older music. Recover the principle it guards: man may not minish what God has given — neither the daily bread of the weak nor the whole counsel of His word — and the God who minishes the proud does it to exalt the humble.
roots_summary: A shortened elder of ‘diminish,’ from the Latin minuere, to make small.
roots_lines: minuere (Latin) — to make small, to lessen; the root of a whole family of smallness-words.
minish — the older, prefix-less English form; to lessen, reduce, bring low.
diminish — the same verb with di- prefixed, which in time all but swallowed ‘minish.’
Kin: minor, minute, minimum, minister (a lesser one) — all from the sense of the small.
The Hebrew of Exo 5:19 (gara) means to clip or withdraw — to shave off from what was due.
usage: Pharaoh would not minish the quota though he took away the straw.
God minishes the proud and brings them low, that He may raise the poor.
Take heed to minish nothing from His word: what He gives, keep whole.
